newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Unisource out to prove it means business - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Unisource out to prove it means business - analysts.

text.p: A plan by European telecoms joint venture Unisource NV to merge its three partners' international networks is a sign it believes it can hold its own as a global player after recent upheavals, investment bankers and analysts said.

Unisource on Wednesday said it agreed to merge the international networks of partners PTT Telecom of the Netherlands, Telia of Sweden and Swiss Telecom PTT to create a company with a $2.0 billion a year turnover.

"The most important thing is that it is a stronger glue with which to bind the alliance together, and is part of Unisource's medium-term campaign to demonstrate its underlying strength to the market," said Paul Staples, an investment banker at Schroders in London.

Unisource plans big economies of scale by bundling together its partners' international networks, stripping out duplications of switches, connections and network management centres in a move which it says can deliver cost savings of 20-30 percent.

Industry observers have suggested that Unisource's future has been clouded by the move in April by Telefonica de Espana to leave the group, and reports that partner AT&T Corp was in merger talks with U.S. regional telecoms firm SBC Communications Inc.
Unisource has a 60/40 joint venture with AT&T called AT&T Unisource which offers business communications.

The departure of Telefonica, and with it potential access to lucrative Latin American markets, was seen as weakening the appeal of Unisource to AT&T. News later that AT&T was mulling a merger with SBC further raised questions about AT&T's plans.
"Unisource has sent out a signal to the rest of the industry that it is not about to be disbanded," said Staples.
"I wouldn't describe it as a serious risk but there was a slight concern that without clear guidance from AT&T and with Telefonica gone Unisource was in a comparatively weak position," he added.

Analysts said Unisource had to prove it could perform against its main rivals Concert, which groups British Telecom Plc and MCI Communications, and Global One, the alliance between France Telecom, Deutsche Telekom and Sprint of the United States.

"There is more than a symbolic importance to the announcement because you are seeing network integration as a much more visible committment than the first generation of alliance structures where you just had marketing agreements, or distribution agreements plus or minus some equity participations which could be fairly easily bought or sold," said Staples.

"I think it's fair to say Unisource and others are quite concerned about the potential for playing a game of musical chairs and I think the market is also looking for evidence that these global alliances are more than interesting strategic concepts but are commercially effective," he said.
Other analysts said Unisource was tackling perceptions that it was only a loose alliance, which could be damaging as it competed with Concert and Global One.
"The integration means the cooperation they have will be even stronger," said analyst Peter Wortel of Delta Lloyd Bank.
"There has, however, been criticism that there was a loose alliance between these operators, so that might be another reason they're doing this," he said.

But he added that the Telefonica news and the concerns about AT&T's intentions, coupled with news on Tuesday that PTT Telecom head Ben Verwaayen had been appointed as an executive vice president at Lucent Technologies Inc, remained worrying.
"In my view Telefonica leaving Unisource and AT&T apparently concentrating more on North America will be of more influence than this further integration," he said.
Douglas Wight, analyst at Salomon Brothers in London said he too was concerned by news that Verwaayen, chairman of AT&T Unisource's supervisory board, was leaving.
"It's not great news for either KPN (Dutch PTT) or Unisource that one of the best telecoms managers in the business is leaving," said Wight.
